title: Embracing the Rave
summary: Stu Mackenzie and Joey Walker discuss the band’s improvised modular rave set, upcoming orchestral performances and the possibilities opened by playing without a fixed script.
transcript:
Stu Mackenzie and Joey Walker of King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios, the day before the band's first Australian rave set, a free show at Federation Square. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 23 October 2025. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: And of course, as you mentioned at the top, Lauren: 27 albums in so far, not counting all of the unofficials and the bootlegs. Over the course of 15 years, you’ve built a really vast catalogue of albums, but even more than that, something of a musical universe, the Gizzverse, that people would know. The albums you produce always follow their own path. You’ve got your own label, p(doom) Records, which lets you explore microtonal rock, thrash metal, long-form jazz improvisation and so much more.

The most recent album, Phantom Island, which we were just listening to, came out in June with some beautiful orchestral arrangements, which are just stunning. And we couldn’t be more excited to hear that you’ve been developing some electronic rave sets, too. The first one in Australia is tomorrow night at Fed Square, with DJ Merve supporting. So we want to ask: where was this idea born, this new chapter of electronic rave music?

Stu: Sick. It’s probably been — thanks for the very epic intro as well. We just make music, mostly, which makes sense. But it’s been something that’s been coming together for a few years, and simmering away in the background for probably quite a lot of years before that as well. I think we had this goal to try and figure out how to make live improvised techno with six people, which seems hard, and is extremely hard. It actually is hard. So I think we’re starting to find the spot within that universe that makes sense for us.

Lauren: By coincidence, the week you’re playing your first local rave set, Tame Impala dropped their new rave album as well. It feels like there’s something in the air at the moment. Were you channelling a feeling of needing to dance and release energy?

Joey: I mean, yes and no. It has, as you said, been simmering away. Butterfly 3000: there wasn’t a single acoustic instrument on that record. It’s all just synthesisers. But it wasn’t a dance album. And then the remix album was amazing, the artists that came aboard for that, which is crazy.

And then during the pandemic, I got into Eurorack modular synthesising, which has kind of been an endgame for me for a really long time. That’s the format. For people out there, it’s just the funny-looking synth with heaps of cables on it: synthesiser guts, with the cables on the outside.

So during a normal Gizzard show, I would have my little Eurorack synth on stage, and I’d contribute in that way. And then we made the record The Silver Cord, which was kind of this, I don’t know, Frankenstein genre of electronic music, whatever that was. And then I guess Stu kind of inevitably — I was like, ‘Man, this modular thing seems like —’

Stu: And I was like, ‘Nah, it’s boring. Stop talking about it all the time.’

Joey: And then, classic Stu, he just kind of started from nothing, and now could have a modular synthesis YouTube channel dedicated to it.

Lauren: We heard it’s hard to find you anywhere but in front of your synthesisers at the moment. You’ve said your recent obsession with Eurorack modular synthesis feels like discovering guitar as a teenager all over again. Is that right?

Stu: Yeah, it does. I had this realisation that the feeling is really similar to when I first started playing guitar, and it felt like the universe was massive, and that you could do anything with this instrument. That’s how I remember feeling as a teenager, first learning to play guitar. And I think I have that same feeling now, and it’s good. I kind of try and chase that, actually, making music. And it’s cool when you latch onto something like that. I remember when we started doing microtonal music, there was a similar feeling of the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow, sort of thing. But yeah, we try to chase that thing.

Lauren: What does it look and sound like in the studio when you’re messing with these cables? I have an impression of what Eurorack modular synthesis looks like, but in your world, what does it look like? Is it controlled chaos?

Joey: Really funny. It’s like a crime scene. It’s so hectic. Our sound guy, who lives in Byron Bay, arrived today for the show tomorrow, and he just walked in and he was like, ‘Oh my God.’ But yeah, we’re all on a big table, and we have our modulars, each of our synths, A-framed together. So me and Stu are back to back. It’s a giant pyramid. Yeah, it’s a pyramid.

And then Ambrose and Cookie are kind of joined, and Lucas is on the end of the table as well. And then Cavs, the drummer, is on the kit. He was kind of the last to the party; he was just like, ‘Shut up.’ But then Stu built him a little drum machine Eurorack kit. And Cavs was like, ‘All right, all right.’ Kind of walked into the studio and caught him just trying to get a patch cable, and he turned around and he was so embarrassed. But no, we’re all there.

So the thing, I guess, is we have the songs we’re playing, which would be from The Silver Cord, or some other songs that we’re retrofitting to this setup, and they’re in a very simple form. Maybe it’s a key melody that everyone’s receiving, which is maybe the binding sinew of the song. But outside of that, it’s completely improvised in the moment. And the great thing with modular is that it’s very generative. We don’t want to go into a tech deep dive here, but essentially it’s really good at manifesting and creating melody and rhythm and whatever, pulling it out of thin air, really.

So it’s kind of like a dance with each other, of how we interact in that moment, and it’s hard enough doing that with one person, let alone two, but with six people doing it, it’s a lot. It’s a dance, to let things breathe and all that stuff. So it’s been really good, and I feel like we’re at a really exciting point with it all. It also feels infinite, I feel like, in terms of where we can take it. But yeah, we’re nervous for tomorrow, but we’re excited.

Lauren: In addition to this rave set, you’ve been touring three distinct shows simultaneously: the rock, orchestral and electronic rave sets. You’ll be back in December for the orchestra show on December 12, and there’s a rock show the next night as well. Can you tell us the difference between them from your perspective, maybe even in terms of the preparation and performance behind them?

Stu: The orchestra shows are, I feel like, for us as a band, probably furthest from what we’re used to. We have to play to charts, and we’ve got 30-odd people behind us who are playing to a script, which is not the way we tend to operate. We’ve worked out a really fun way of doing it, though, because we’ve done quite a few of the orchestra shows now. But yeah, we have to be more of a cog in the machine. And that’s fun. It’s different. It requires discipline. Whereas the usual show is not discipline-based. It’s actually a lack of discipline that usually works the best with the band.

Joey: And one thing I realised as well, with the orchestra show versus a traditional Gizzard show: we were on tour a month or two ago in America, doing primarily the orchestra stuff, but then we’d have a normal rock show in between. Going into the orchestra thing, it was very unfamiliar. We didn’t know what to expect. We were all very nervous, dealing with these professional musicians and stuff like that. But once we got over that initial feeling, and realised it is what it is, once we’re there, we don’t really have to worry about it. The variables aren’t as much of a thing.

And then going into a normal Gizzard show, I was like, ‘Oh wow, the amount of work,’ I guess mental work, at least how I feel going into a Gizzard show, because it’s so last minute; every set’s different. Tonight Stu will be like, ‘We’re going to play this song.’ I don’t even know what that song’s called. I haven’t heard that song in however long. So there’s so much energy put into a normal Gizzard show, which I think at the end of the day really pays off for us, and hopefully for the audience: that frenetic, chaotic feel. But it was interesting to see that duality between this very regimented orchestral thing and a normal Gizzard show. It was cool. It’s refreshing, I think.

Lauren: And you worked with the conductor Sarah Hicks, I think it was, and the composer and music director Chad Kelly on the orchestra tour. How did they change how you think about your own music?

Stu: Yeah, I’ve actually known Chad for quite a few years. Our wives are friends, actually, so I met Chad just at dinner parties and stuff like that. Chad’s a Manchester chap who married an Aussie, but he’s a conductor and a composer and such an incredible musician. We would get together on these dinner party dates and talk about microtonal music and dorky stuff like that, and it was really rad. But we do very much exist on very opposite ends of the musical spectrum. I think we’re both interested in deeply dorky stuff, which is where we connected. But I’m a musical idiot, and he’s a smart musical person. But we find we meet in the middle.

Anyway, we had some opportunities to play some live shows in the States with an orchestra. The idea was to retrofit the back catalogue and do some shows with some amazing top orchestras in the States. And of course we were just like, ‘Well, we have to take that. What a cool opportunity.’ So the first person I called was Chad, to get his take on the whole thing. And I think after speaking with him, and after brainstorming a little bit, it just became obvious that if we want to do one show, we may as well do a tour. And if we’re going to do a tour, we may as well make an album. So Chad really helped with the whole process, and he wrote the charts for Phantom Island and what became of that. And he’s touring with us in Europe as the conductor for the shows.

Joey: And Sarah Hicks did the US stuff, and she’s so incredible as well. I have so much respect for conductors now. I just never knew what they were doing with their little magic wands. But now I feel like I do, and it’s an incredible job, being able to communicate with all of the different musicians, and especially working with a rock band, they have to understand what we’re all doing. It’s like understanding different languages.

Stu: And Sarah is such an amazing conductor. She had this ability to relay this information to every person in a different language, essentially, one by one. It’s very cool. A very, very impressive skill.

Lauren: You’ve also been playing some pretty special places in Europe recently. Back in May you played a former prison in Lithuania, I think it was, that’s been converted into a music venue. Can we ask about the logistics of that, and also what the selection process is like for choosing these locations?

Joey: I mean, the logistics: it was kind of like, let’s do a tour that’s destination-based. In terms of the intensity of what that tour was like, we did five different places, three nights in each place. So for us, it was pretty low impact, which was really nice, to just be in a place. And they were really amazing places. So actually it was kind of good for the old mental health.

Lauren: Because you’d be accustomed to travelling rapidly from place to place.

Joey: It’s just the stereotype of waking up in a car park type thing, in the bus behind the venue, and you have no idea where you are. Yeah, it’s kind of weird. But yeah, that was really cool. It was just really, really amazing. The venues brought so much energy to the shows. We did the one at Lycabettus Hill, which was the second highest point in Athens, other than the hill that the Acropolis is on. And just up there at sunset, it was just insane how cool it was.

Simon: Briefly, we’d like to flip to the recordings you’ve been working on. Phantom Island was the most recent record, written during the same sessions as Flight b741. You’ve described making Phantom Island as adding a new colour and energy to the songs, and you’ve talked a bit about working with Sarah Hicks and Chad Kelly. But can you talk a bit more about the themes and ideas you’re exploring on this record?

Joey: I mean, yeah, musically, it was very cool to work with an orchestra. It does actually feel like you’re painting with, let’s say, a different set of colours, especially for a rock band. And the stuff we were doing on that record was pretty bare bones. We were thinking back to basics. There were no guitar pedals; we were saying, it’s the music that comes out of your fingertips. It’s just trying to be simple, and trying to be the organic version of the guitar, and that sort of thing. And having so many different colours and sounds to play with in the orchestra is very, very cool. But yeah, Chad Kelly arranged amazing stuff for it.

Stu: I feel like, thematically, it’s pretty obvious. But it’s kind of just talking about up to where we are now: just how transient, I guess, our lives have become and stuff. And we all have families, for the most part, so it’s a little bit of an examination of that kind of thing. It felt pretty honest and personal for a record for us, I think. And we were probably challenging ourselves and each other to see how earnest you could get away with being on a rock track like that.

Lauren: In terms of challenging yourselves: in the past, you’ve said you deliberately make yourselves uncomfortable creatively, like using cheap gear, and forcing yourselves into unfamiliar genres. Is that still the case? Or are there other strategies you use to maintain your creativity and your prolific output?

Stu: Well, for this record, I definitely didn’t tell Chad or any of the orchestral players at the time, but we mixed down to an 8-track cassette tape, which is a very cool machine from the ’80s, which is extremely broken. Think about an extremely hi-fi, big orchestra, and we recorded it properly this time. And, by the way, we mixed down to a tiny cassette. That actually felt like a huge challenge. And it was kind of the game. The game was to see how good you could get the tape to sound, actually. So it’s just, I don’t know why I do this.

Joey: There’s also a little bit of trying to subvert doing an orchestral record. It comes with its own kind of — not baggage, but it has a feeling to it. You’re like, ‘Okay, that’s that.’ And very often, when bands do that, it can really not be their best work. So I feel like there was a little bit of a subversion into, like, let’s garage-ify it. You know what I mean? Which is cool. If it was this ultra hi-fi kind of thing, I just think it might have, I don’t know, lost a bit of its soul, or at least a bit of our spirit. I think it’s always trying to inject the Gizzard thing into it.

Stu: It was also genuinely a very, very hard record to finish. I think it had a bit to do with the combination: we were in blues band formation, really, and fusing that with a small orchestra. I think we had 30-odd people in the studio for the orchestral recording. So it was really hard to make that fit. And I think this slightly sadistic way of mixing a record made it make sense, actually. It made it live in the same world.

Joey: And I think also, back to your initial question, in terms of creative impetus or whatever: b741 and Phantom Island came from the same session, in terms of the original tracks on both those albums. But that was a response to the albums we’d had, which were very jammy and nebulous, where the process was a lot of post-production distillation of these huge, expansive jams that we’d do, and then trying to build songs out of them. So it was like, ‘Okay, once we’d gotten through that, we just want to make a song with a couple of chords.’ And that’s what that is.

And so now, coming out the other side of that, everyone has absurd modular synthesisers. You know what I mean? So it is that thing. We are chasing — once something’s cauterised, we kind of try and do the opposite, or what feels the most exciting.

Simon: Is it 27 albums in the last 14, 15 years or so? You’ve covered, as I mentioned earlier, so many genres: thrash metal, synth pop, jazz, electronic rave. Is there a genre you’re excited, or perhaps scared, to attempt?

Stu: I think for the most part we probably aren’t thinking in terms of genre. I mean, maybe we are occasionally. I think we’re genuinely chasing that feeling. We’re chasing the dragon of the hard thing, probably, or the thing that would make us, yeah, scared a little bit, or motivated enough to, yeah, just, I don’t know.

Joey: It can kind of manifest on the technical side: being scared of the learning curve that comes with learning how to use a modular synth. I have a background in dance music, or electronic music, and Stu’s just got hyper-focused. But for a lot of the other guys, it’s like, ‘I guess we’re doing modular synthesis now.’ So there’s trying to inject some form of learning curve that’s cool to try and tackle.

Stu: I think it’s trying to put in these restrictions, these barriers within a framework, so that once we decide, ‘Okay, cool, this album might be metal, or it might be ultra-proggy, or it might be electronic,’ we just set these things. There are all these channels or lanes in between. If we try and narrow —

Joey: Yeah, make it make sense.

Stu: And once we realise what that is, that’s when we’re like, ‘Let’s make the album.’ And then it happens really quickly, because it’s almost like working out what we’re not doing. Sometimes there can be a lot of time before we start anything, or we just talk about it and figure out what exactly the intent is. It’s also just sometimes fun to just burn the house down and start again. And, yeah, I think there’s an element of that, too.

Simon: Well, it is so thrilling to be a fan of your work, because there’s always that sense of exhilaration, excitement and entering into the unknown. Something we wanted to talk to you about before we let you go is the community you’ve built through your tireless work ethic. The Weirdo Swarm track the shows they’ve attended, organise meet-ups, run charity events, and take part in an annual gift exchange called Gizzmas. It’s a beautiful community that you’ve built over so many years. We were just wondering how much you get to engage with that at all, and where it fits within your working schedules.

Stu: For me, when you talk about that stuff, it is pretty abstract, for the most part. It’s actually quite a strange and unreal concept to truly understand. And I feel like the thing I’ve said before, especially when we were talking about the record b741, which had a lot of flying-on-planes metaphors: a lot of it does feel like being in an aeroplane. If you actually think about the fact that you are in the sky, you actually might have a panic attack. And playing to the kind of audiences we’re lucky enough to play to now, I have to abstract myself from it, because it just actually doesn’t do any good to think too hard about what the broader ecosystem is.

However, I do really like talking to people, and I’ll always try and chat with folks and get a sense of what is going on on the ground.

Joey: And that’s when it feels real.

Stu: I think we do, yeah. That is our interaction. We do have a lot of people across the world who might be figures within the Gizz fan community, who we honestly do talk to; they talk to our managers, we talk to them. There’s an exchange of relationship.

But for the most part, I think, as to the whole lore of the whole thing, I think if we were to actually stop and engage, it would kind of cease to exist. I think we just let it exist, and it’s there because we’re not engaging with it. We’re just doing our thing. And we just like making music with each other. It’s as simple as that. We actually just like being in the same room as each other and making music together. That’s the thing.
